newsitem.title: INDIA: Suicide protest casts pall over Miss World in India.
newsitem.headline: Suicide protest casts pall over Miss World in India.

text.p: The Miss World show will go on in India despite the suicide of a man who set himself ablaze in protest against the beauty pageant, organisers said on Friday.

"We are sad for his family and friends. It is sad for any human being. But in no way did we accredit it to what we are doing," Eric Morley, British founder of the Miss World contest 45-years ago, told Reuters from Bangalore.
In the south Indian city where Miss World will be crowned on November 23, a 1,000 strong demonstration against the beauty contest coming to India passed off peacefully.
The 89 beauty queen contestants awoke in their hotel guarded by around 100 policemen inside and another 100 outside.
Later, they went by bus for a rehearsal at the Chinnaswamy cricket stadium, the venue for the final night, flanked by jeeps of armed police who accompany them everywhere in Bangalore.

Elsewhere in the city, protesters chanted "Down with Miss World," echoing words uttered by Suresh Kumar on Thursday before he lit his kerosene soaked clothes in Madurai, a city 432 kilometres (270 miles) south in neighbouring Tamil Nadhu state.
Kumar's next and last words, according to local reports, were "water, water, water".
By the time onlookers doused the flames he had 90 percent burns.
Right-wing Hindu nationalist party leaders who led the march made no mention of Kumar, an unemployed member of an extremist marxist group, in speeches at the end of the rally.
"My party workers should come from every corner of Karnataka (state) to lay siege to the stadium," Anant Kumar, a Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) member of parliement, exhorted the crowd.
The police had banned rallies involving more than 10 people, but apparently compromised on an orderly demonstration.
"We've had more publicity than before. But it is not the type of publicity anyone would welcome," Morley said.
But the contest did get support from India's famous "Bandit Queen", Phoolan Devi, now a member of parliament after 11 years in jail. She said the BJP was politicising the event.
"What's wrong if the beauty is presented beautifully with Indian touch and style?" the Press Trust of India news agency quoted her as saying.
The organisers have already bowed to local sensitivities by staging the swimsuit parade outside India last weekend.
A series of events held in the run up to the final night have passed off smoothly, albeit under heavy security.
But Kumar's apparent martyrdom has heightened the state of alert in the Bangalore police.

Even before Kumar took his life, the Mahila Jagran Samiti (Forum for Awakening Women) threatened its members would join the audience on the final night and take cyanide to lessen the pain before committing self-immolation.
"We are on guard. It may have repercussions here," G.K. Bekal, Bangalore deputy police commissioner, said.
A judge still has to decide whether the state government can call in crack paramilitary teams to back up 12,000 local police already deployed.
Morley said he had not worked anywhere where the security was so tight, but it was not hampering the event.
"It doesn't really concern us. All I'd say is that it's stopping the girls from going out shopping freely," Morley said.

Opponents of Miss World say the pageant, which raises around $150 million for charity and drew a global television audience of up to two billion last year, degrades women and represents a "cultural invasion".
But polls conducted by a national newspaper have shown little groundswell support for the militants.
